document.outcome: Efficiency of a heat engine; distinction from Carnot efficiency

content.text: In each cycle, a heat engine absorbs 800 J of thermal energy from a hot reservoir at 500 K and transfers 600 J of thermal energy to a cold reservoir at 300 K.
What is the efficiency of the heat engine?
The work is divided by the energy rejected instead of the energy absorbed: 200 / 600 = 0.33
The Carnot efficiency is calculated instead of the actual efficiency: 1 − 300 / 500 = 0.40
The ratio of the energy rejected to the energy absorbed is taken as the efficiency: 600 / 800 = 0.75
Work done per cycle = 800 − 600 = 200 J. Efficiency = useful work / energy absorbed = 200 / 800 = 0.25.

content.text: A fixed mass of a monatomic ideal gas is taken through a cycle A → B → C → A.

- In state A the pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, the volume is 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ and the temperature is 300 K. - A → B is an isobaric expansion to a volume of 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³. The temperature at B is 750 K. - B → C is an adiabatic expansion. The temperature at C is 300 K. - C → A is an isothermal compression.

stimuli.description: Pressure–volume (P–V) graph; not to scale. From A to B a straight horizontal line to the right (constant pressure). From B to C a steep curve going to the right and downwards (adiabatic). From C to A a less steep curve going to the left and upwards (isothermal). The cycle is traversed clockwise.
